{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-06: "maybe a .mcp.json could have the graph_id for reflow2, dynograph-foundation, and flo2...so when any design decision is made, reflow2 can utilize all 3 graphs?"

⭐ EXTENDED THE SAME DAY, AND THE EXTENSION IS WHAT MAKES IT AN ARCHITECTURE RATHER THAN A CONVENIENCE. Anthony's second pass: "projectC is dependent upon projectB which is dependent upon projectA and these are all managed by user1. say user2 is responsible for projectD which is dependent upon projectC. user2's .mcp.json should only have the graph_id for projectC and projectD, while user1's .mcp.json should have projectA, B and C. theoretically, you could link huge projects together with multiple users only managing their respective set of projects."

THE RULE THAT FALLS OUT OF HIS OWN EXAMPLE, and he did not state it explicitly: projectC appears in BOTH configs. So a graph_id in a config does not mean one thing — THE SAME GRAPH IS WRITABLE FOR ITS OWNER AND READABLE FOR ITS CONSUMER. user1 owns C and may write it; user2 depends on C and may only read it. The set a user holds is therefore {the graphs I own → writable} ∪ {the graphs I directly depend on → readable}, and that is not a flat list of equals — it is a list with a role per entry.

THIS RESOLVES THE TENSION THIS NODE WAS RECORDED TO NAME. Option (b) below was written as the conservative choice — one writable graph, N readable. Anthony's federation makes it the GENERAL one: N writable (the ones you own) and M readable (the ones you depend on), which degenerates to (b) for a single-project owner and to today's behaviour for someone with no dependencies. Option (a) — a flat list where every graph is equal — stops being the simple choice once the roles are visible, because it is the only one that has to answer "which of these three does this write land in".

⭐ THE SCALE PROPERTY, which is the real content of "link huge projects together": NOBODY HOLDS THE WHOLE DAG. Each user holds a LOCAL CUT of it — their own subtree plus one hop outward — and the cuts overlap exactly at the ownership seams. That is why it composes to arbitrary size without any user, machine or process ever loading the whole federation, and it is a materially different claim from "one process holds many graphs" (dec:one-process-many-stores), which is about a SERVER holding tenants. This is about a PERSON holding a neighbourhood.

⚠️ THE HONEST LIMIT, and it is the thing worth deciding rather than discovering: user2 sees C but NOT B or A. If user2's need in C turns out to require a change in B, user2 cannot see that and cannot even tell that B exists. The requirement has to RELAY — user2 asks C's owner, who then discovers it is really a B problem. Whether that is a feature (bounded blast radius, matching real ownership and real org charts) or a defect (a need can stall invisibly one hop out of view) is a genuine question. The bounded reading is probably right and is how every package ecosystem already behaves; the cost is that transitive needs travel at the speed of humans, which is exactly the friction Anthony opened this whole thread wanting to remove.

AND IT SHARPENS THE AUTHORITY QUESTION NEXT DOOR: the boundary of authority is EXACTLY the shared graph. Everything dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency asks — who may write intent into a design they do not own — is now localised to the overlap, C. It is not a question about the federation; it is a question about each seam in it, asked once per seam, between two named people.

IT ALSO MAKES OPTION (c) NEXT DOOR ACTUALLY WORK AT SCALE. "The upstream pulls rather than the downstream pushes" needs a reverse index — who declares a dependency on me — which today does not exist because req:design-dependencies-declared points downward only. Under this federation the reverse index is small and local: C's owner asks who declares a dependency on C and finds exactly user2's D, never the whole world.

RELATED AND ALREADY OPEN: dec:idea-cross-org-federation asks whether reflow2 should federate heterogeneous designs across ORGANISATIONS the way OpenMBEE does, rather than composing exports. Anthony's example is the same shape one scale down — across PEOPLE rather than organisations — which is useful, because it means the mechanism can be tried on two brothers and three repos before it has to survive two companies.

⚠️ IT ALSO PULLS AGAINST A DECISION MADE TWELVE HOURS EARLIER. dec:one-process-many-stores (proposed, 2026-08-05) has each client session ATTACHED TO EXACTLY ONE graph, and carries req:a-session-cannot-reach-another-designs-graph as a SECURITY property for flo2: project A's design must be unreachable from project B's session. Both can be true, but only if the distinction is stated rather than discovered later: MULTI-TENANT ISOLATION (strangers' projects on a hosted server, must not see each other) is not the same as COMPOSITION (one author's own interdependent designs, useless apart). The federation above makes the split cleaner than it first looked — isolation is between TENANTS, composition is within one tenant's declared neighbourhood — but nothing in the design says so yet.

IT LANDS ON AN OPEN QUESTION HE HAS ALREADY LEANED ON. dec:how-a-session-is-pointed-at-a-design (proposed) records his 2026-08-05 preference — "I like this approach of just pointing .mcp.json at the graph_id" — and the counter beside it: [BL-123] holds that the /mcp reconnect is the one step an autonomous agent cannot take, so config-file selection is the option an agent cannot exercise for itself. A multi-graph .mcp.json inherits that counter unchanged.

WHAT IS ALREADY BUILT, so the gap is smaller than the question sounds. cap:composed-analysis is REALIZED: two designs analysed together without either being written to, the other's ids namespaced into an in-memory graph, every finding attributed ours / theirs / seam. describe_designs (shipped 2026-08-05) answers what design lives at a path without opening it. So "reason across several graphs" is a call you can make today; what a config would add is that it happens BY DEFAULT and WITHOUT BEING ASKED.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN.

(a) A FLAT LIST OF graph_ids, ALL EQUAL. Closest to the first phrasing. Now the weakest, because the federation example shows the entries are NOT equal and this is the only option that must then answer "which one does a write land in" at every call site.

(b) ROLES PER ENTRY — owned/writable versus depended-on/readable, which is what Anthony's own example describes. Preserves single-writer per graph, preserves the isolation property's shape, matches how every dependency manifest already works, and degenerates gracefully for the one-project case. Counter: it does not by itself serve the flo2 case, because flo2's need is for something to be written INTO reflow2 — that is dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency, not this node.

(c) NOTHING IN CONFIG — composition stays an explicit call against a dependency declared in the manifest, where req:design-dependencies-declared already puts it. Cheapest and already built. Counter: an explicit call is one somebody has to remember to make, which is the failure req:no-idea-goes-quiet exists to reject.

(d) THE MANIFEST, NOT .mcp.json, IS THE RIGHT FILE — and the federation strengthens this considerably. reflow2 ALREADY declares its dynograph-foundation dependency this way, pinned and version-checked, with ver:design-dependencies-declared passing against the real thing. A DEPENDENCY IS A PROPERTY OF THE DESIGN, NOT OF THE MACHINE SOMEBODY READS IT ON: projectD depends on projectC no matter whose laptop is open, so putting it in .mcp.json — per-machine, and gitignored in this very repo — means every clone and every teammate re-states it, which is the shadow-list failure in a new costume. The counter, and it is real: the manifest says what the DESIGN depends on, while .mcp.json says what THIS PERSON is working on, and Anthony's user1/user2 split is genuinely about people. Those may both be needed — a committed manifest for the dependency edges, a per-user config for which subtree you have in hand.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SHARPENED 2026-08-12 — THE UNION FRAMING, AND THE FIRST TRIAL EVIDENCE
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, thinking out loud, and he said "it is just an idea".

HIS WORDS: "as I own both reflow2 and flo2, I'd like to get to the point I can work in either project and changes I make in one project are automatically related to one another (maybe like there are external interface nodes that for a given session, allows you to treat the union of 2+ reflow2 graphs as one graph for that reflow2 session)."

⭐ DELIBERATELY SHARPENED RATHER THAN FORKED. This is the same question this node already holds; forking would be the near-duplicate the search-first rule exists to prevent. THREE THINGS ARE GENUINELY NEW in his framing:

1. **UNION, not read-across.** Everything above is about REASONING across graphs — compose, analyse, attribute ours/theirs/seam. He is asking for the graphs to BE one graph for the duration of a session, which is a stronger claim: not "I can see both" but "there is no seam to see".
2. **EXTERNAL INTERFACE NODES as the mechanism.** A named thing in each graph that says "this is where I join". The federation model above has roles per graph but no vocabulary for the join itself.
3. **AUTOMATIC RELATING ON WRITE.** "changes I make in one project are automatically related to one another" — the existing text is read-side. This is the write side, and it is where the cost lives.

═══ THE TRIAL EVIDENCE, 2026-08-12 — the first time pairing actually computed on this pair ═══

`pair_designs` was run for real, reflow2 against flo2's committed export. Result: **paired 0, conflicts 10, unmet_needs 5, dead_surface 2, candidates 1, unclassified 2 ours / 1 theirs.** Three findings, and all three argue FOR the union rather than against it.

⭐⭐ (A) THE SEAM COULD NOT COMPUTE, AND NOT FOR A FIXABLE REASON. Zero pairs — because flo2 models `cmp:reflow2-service` as a component it CONTAINS, providing `ifc:reflow2-design-api` to its own `cmp:tool-loop`. Pairing matches complements ACROSS a boundary; flo2 drew reflow2 INSIDE its boundary, so there is no boundary. That is a legitimate model (Anthony builds that half) and it makes the seam permanently uncomputable. **A UNION DISSOLVES THIS ENTIRELY** — if the two graphs are one for the session, containment is just containment and needs no complement.

⭐⭐⭐ (B) THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT FOR THE UNION, FOUND BY ACCIDENT: TWO GRAPHS CAN AGREE BY BEING IDENTICALLY WRONG. Both designs label the reflow2 boundary `medium: REST`; both MEAN MCP, and both say so in `spec` prose where nothing computes. Had the roles been complementary they would have PAIRED — on a shared falsehood — and reported a clean seam. The tool defends against `unspecified` reading as agreement; it has no defence against both sides stating the same wrong value. **A SHARED NODE CANNOT DISAGREE WITH ITSELF.** The entire class of seam-mismatch defects (medium, auth, transport_security, payload) exists only because the contract is TWO nodes that must be kept in agreement. One node has no agreement to maintain. That is the real argument for external interface nodes, and it is stronger than the convenience one Anthony opened with.

🛑 (C) BUT THE SUBSTRATE HE WOULD BE UNIONING IS THE WRONG ONE FOR THIS CONSUMER. A backtest replayed reflow2's history against the two places flo2's hand-written tracker went stale, and measured which signal would have caught them:
  - The TOOLSNAP diff caught both input-contract changes decisively and mechanically (`inputSchema.properties` {} → {contributor_id}).
  - The DESIGN EXPORT diff buried them: 1 relevant node in 70 changes, then 12 in 103.
  - NEITHER caught the result-shape change (`suggested_fix_type` → Option) — toolsnaps record `annotations, description, inputSchema, name` and NO output schema at all.
  - ⚠️ AND THE DESIGN EXPORT ACTIVELY LIED: `cap:owed-to-a-contributor` reads `in_progress` at v0.26.1, v0.27.0 AND v0.28.0, three releases after the capability shipped, because status moves only on the owner's word and nobody went back. A subscription built on it would have told flo2 "still in progress" about working code — worse than silence.
  ⇒ **flo2 consumes reflow2's TOOL SURFACE, not its DESIGN.** Unioning the design graphs joins the wrong two things for that dependency. It would be right for a sibling consuming reflow2's INTENT. So "link two projects" is at least two different links, and the union answers one of them.

═══ WHAT THE UNION NEWLY COSTS, which the read-side framing above never had to answer ═══

- **WHICH GRAPH DOES A WRITE LAND IN?** Option (a) above was already noted as the one that must answer this; the union makes it unavoidable rather than optional. A new node created "in the union" has no home until someone says which.
- **TWO STORES, TWO LOCKS.** `req:single-writer-graph` gives each directory an exclusive RocksDB lock. A session writing across a union holds two, and lock ordering between them is a real concurrency design, not a detail.
- **WHOSE EXPORT CARRIES A SHARED NODE?** If an external interface node is genuinely one node, both repos' exports either carry it (and now disagree on every unrelated commit) or neither does (and it lives nowhere durable). This is the phantom-drift problem at repo scale, and `dec:export-once-per-pr` exists because that problem is already hard within ONE repo.
- **WHO ACCEPTS INTENT IN THE OVERLAP?** `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` is unambiguous with one owner per graph. In a union owned by one person it stays simple — which is exactly why Anthony's own case is the right first trial — and it is undefined the moment the union spans two people.

═══ WHAT IS ALREADY BUILT TOWARD IT ═══

`compose_and_analyse` is REALIZED and does the READ-ONLY union today: it imports the other design into an in-memory graph, NAMESPACES their ids so nothing overwrites, throws it away, and attributes every finding ours / theirs / seam. So the union already exists for reads and is thrown away; his idea is that it persists for a session and accepts writes. The namespacing is the part that would have to change, because a shared node is precisely one that must NOT be namespaced apart.

NOT DECIDED. ⭐ THE CHEAPEST NEXT TRIAL, since it needs no new vocabulary: take the ONE boundary that should be shared (reflow2's `ifc:mcp-tools` and flo2's `ifc:reflow2-design-api`), and see what breaks if it is treated as one node rather than two — which export carries it, what happens when one side edits it, and whether the medium disagreement becomes impossible or merely relocated.

═══ SHARPENED AGAIN 2026-08-12 — MUTABLE / IMMUTABLE, AND THE TOOL THAT ALREADY DOES IT ═══

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING. Anthony, on what happens when he does NOT own the other project: "maybe I can still import, just all changes have to be in one side of the graph. basically, treat one side as unchangeable. this is like: mutable objects can change their internal state or value after creation, while immutable objects cannot be altered once they are created."

⭐ THE FRAMING COLLAPSES THREE OF THE FOUR COSTS THE UNION SECTION ABOVE RAISED, and that is why it is worth recording rather than merely noting:
  - WHICH GRAPH DOES A WRITE LAND IN? — gone. Only one side accepts writes.
  - TWO STORES, TWO LOCKS — gone. You hold one write lock; the other side is a document.
  - WHOSE EXPORT CARRIES A SHARED NODE? — gone. Yours does, marked foreign.
  - WHO MAY ACCEPT INTENT IN THE OVERLAP? — gone, and elegantly: you CANNOT move intent in a design you are structurally unable to write. `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` stops being a discipline someone must remember and becomes enforced by construction.

🛑🛑 AND IT IS ALREADY BUILT. `mirror_surface` (dec:nested-graphs option (c)) mirrors another design's published surface in as FOREIGN NODES stamped with the coordinate — `mirror_of`, `mirror_content_hash`, `mirrored_at`, `provenance: imported`. Its own description states the design choice that makes the union work: "foreignness is a property of the node rather than of the link", so local components provides/consumes the mirrored Interface with ORDINARY edges and the golden thread, propagate and every detector work unchanged. `mirrors` reads the coordinate back as "a dated claim about a VERSION of another design, never a live truth". COLLISIONS ARE REFUSED rather than merged.

⇒ Under Anthony's standing triage rule this half is SATISFIED and needs nothing new.

🛑 THE MEASUREMENT THAT REFRAMES THIS WHOLE THREAD, taken 2026-08-12: **ZERO MIRRORED NODES EXIST IN EITHER GRAPH.** No node in reflow2's design or flo2's carries `mirror_of`. `mirror_surface`, `export_surface`, `pair_designs`, `seam_report` and `mirrors` are all built, shipped, and have never once been run on a real pair and kept. That is precisely `cap:built-and-consumed-by-nothing`'s shape — built, correct, consumed by nothing — found on the linking layer the same day that detector shipped.

⇒ **SO THE CONCEPT WORK HERE IS NOT SPECIFYING SOMETHING TO BUILD. IT IS DISCOVERING WHY SOMETHING ALREADY BUILT WAS NEVER PICKED UP.** On today's evidence the answer is the bilateral precondition: mirroring needs the far side to have declared a published surface, and reflow2 declared no `required` interface at all until PR #130. Neither party gets value until both have paid.

⚠️ WHAT IMMUTABILITY DOES NOT SOLVE — it RELOCATES staleness into a refresh, and refresh is where the sharp edges are:
  - A mirror is a SNAPSHOT. Immutable means you cannot edit it; it does not mean it is current.
  - REFRESH REPLACES THE IMMUTABLE SIDE WHOLESALE — clean, like updating a lockfile.
  - BUT YOUR EDGES POINT INTO THEIR NODES. If they delete or rename something you consume, a refresh leaves your edges dangling — and reflow2 now REFUSES dangling edges outright. So a refresh can fail on referential integrity. Whether that is a refusal, a report or a gap is undecided and is the first thing a trial should exercise.
  - VENDOR OR REFERENCE? Does your committed export CARRY their mirrored nodes (self-contained and reproducible, but their churn appears in your diffs) or merely NAME them by `mirror_of` + `mirror_content_hash` (small, but your export alone is unreadable)? This is the vendoring-versus-lockfile question every package ecosystem faces. `mirror_content_hash` suggests the design already leans to the first with the second's guarantee.

THE CHEAPEST TRIAL, needing no new vocabulary and nothing enduring: mirror flo2's published surface into a SCRATCH reflow2 graph and run the tool that exists. Learn what the coordinate supports, then mirror a SECOND time with the far side moved, and see what happens to edges pointing at a node that changed.

THE TRIAL PROPOSED ABOVE WAS RUN, 2026-08-12 — AND IT FOUND A DEFECT
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

The section above ended: "mirror flo2's published surface into a SCRATCH reflow2 graph and run the tool that exists. Learn what the coordinate supports, then mirror a SECOND time with the far side moved." Done. Read-only against both real stores — flo2's graph was NEVER OPENED, because opening a store writes a schema stamp and would have silently upgraded his other project from 0.27.0; its committed export was imported into a scratch graph instead.

⭐ THE FIRST MIRROR IS CLEAN, AND THE BLACK BOX IS REAL. `export_surface` on flo2 gave 5 boundaries / 13 nodes exposed, 93 nodes and 201 edges WITHHELD as internal. `mirror_surface` took it: **13 nodes, 19 edges, ZERO collisions**, pinned to `mirror_content_hash sha256:0463d397…`. What arrived was 1 Project, 6 Components, 5 Interfaces, 1 Artifact, with **5 CONTAINS edges from `proj:flo2`** plus PROVIDES/CONSUMES/SPECIFIES — i.e. A PROJECT NODE CONTAINING ITS PARTS, with its published interfaces as ports. Then `cmp:service CONSUMES ifc:reflow2-design-api` was drawn as an ORDINARY local edge into a foreign node and worked exactly as the tool's description promises.

📌 TWO DETAILS THE DESCRIPTION DOES NOT SAY. Mirrored ids are NOT NAMESPACED — `ifc:reflow2-design-api` sits beside reflow2's own ids, and safety comes from collisions being REFUSED rather than from prefixing (unlike `compose_and_analyse`, which namespaces). And the COORDINATE IS NOT ON THE NODE: a mirrored node carries only `provenance: imported`; `mirror_of` / `mirror_content_hash` / `mirrored_at` live on the mirrored PROJECT, read back by `mirrors`. So a node cannot say whose it is without tracing to its Project, and `imported` is the same value a plain restore-from-backup sets — the two are indistinguishable at the node.

🛑🛑 THE SECOND MIRROR IS THE FINDING: **`mirror_surface` HAS NO REFRESH.** The far side was moved the way a real partner moves — `ifc:reflow2-design-api` renamed to `ifc:reflow2-tool-surface`, `medium` corrected REST → unspecified — and mirrored again:

    mirrored_nodes        1
    mirrored_edges        0
    collisions           12      <- everything from the first mirror
    mirror_content_hash  null

**Twelve of thirteen ids were refused as collisions WITH THE PREVIOUS MIRROR OF THE SAME DESIGN.** The refusal is correct and protective for a genuine cross-design clash, and its message says exactly that — "Two designs using one id for different things is a naming conversation between their owners" — but that is not what happened, and the guard cannot tell the two cases apart.

THE RESULTING STATE IS QUIETLY WRONG, which is what makes this worse than a plain failure:
  - the STALE `ifc:reflow2-design-api` is still present, still `medium: REST`, still the old name;
  - the renamed `ifc:reflow2-tool-surface` also arrived, with ZERO edges (`mirrored_edges: 0`), so it is orphaned;
  - the host's own `CONSUMES` edge STILL POINTS AT THE STALE NODE, and nothing said it moved;
  - **`mirrors` still reports the FIRST hash and `mirrored_at: 2026-08-12`** — so after a failed refresh the staleness register READS FRESH. The whole value of `mirror_content_hash` is the tool's own claim that "a newer surface with a different hash means this mirror is stale", and a silent no-op leaves the consumer believing they are current when they are two changes behind.

⇒ **RE-MIRRORING ONE `mirror_of` IS A DIFFERENT OPERATION FROM MIRRORING A NEW DESIGN.** One is "replace what I hold of theirs, at a new pin"; the other is "add a stranger, and refuse anything that clashes". Only the second is implemented, and the first is what a standing subscription is made of. This is the sharp edge the mutable/immutable framing predicted — immutability makes the first import clean and relocates the whole problem into refresh — and it is worse than predicted, because refresh is not awkward, it is absent.

📌 AND IT EXPLAINS THE ZERO-INSTANCE FINDING. The layer was built, exercised on a FIRST mirror, and never run twice — so the missing half was never visible. `cap:built-and-consumed-by-nothing` finds things nothing consumes; this is the adjacent failure, a capability consumed exactly once and therefore only half-tested.

⚠️ NOT ESTABLISHED BY THIS TRIAL, so the result is not read wider than it is: whether a refresh SHOULD replace, merge, or refuse-and-report; what should happen to a host edge whose foreign target was renamed or withdrawn (reflow2 now refuses dangling edges outright, so a replace-style refresh has to answer this); and whether the host's committed export should CARRY mirrored nodes or merely NAME them by pin.
